idiom_name: NavigationStack + NavigationPath (or a screen enum in an @Observable model)
implementation_notes: SwiftUI removes the retained view objects: views are values derived from state, so the handler role is the navigation state itself - a NavigationPath (or a screen enum in an @Observable model) decides which screen exists, navigationDestination maps a value to its view, and switching is appending or removing a value on the path. Syncing is automatic because every view reads the model it is handed; there is nothing to register, dispose or notify, and no dangling handle by construction. The classic retained structure is still justified in SwiftUI only where a screen must be kept alive while off-screen (a long-running editor, a live session), which is expressed by keeping that state in a model object outside the view instead of retaining the view. Choose the UIKit variant when the codebase is imperative or when the stack must be manipulated directly.
pitfalls: Views are value types recreated on every state change: anything that must survive navigation (unsaved text, selected tab, scroll position) belongs in an @Observable model, not in @State inside the destination view.
A path element must be a value (Hashable enum or id), never a reference to a view - putting view objects in the path mixes lifecycle with navigation state.
Deep stacks re-evaluate bodies often, so heavy work in a body (queries, formatting) must be hoisted into the model or it runs on every redraw.

variants.name: UIKit UINavigationController stack (classic)
variants.idiom_name: UINavigationController.viewControllers + push/pop; UITabBarController for parallel views
variants.implementation_notes: UIKit's navigation controller is the textbook view handler: viewControllers is the ordered registry of live screens, pushViewController creates and activates one, popViewController and popToRootViewController dispose the ones above, and setViewControllers replaces the whole set in a single command - with UITabBarController covering the 'several views alive, one active' case and UIWindowScene.windows listing the scene's windows. Screens are view-controller objects retained by the stack and released when popped. Choose this variant for existing UIKit code or when navigation must be imperative (custom transitions, programmatic stack surgery).
pitfalls: A popped view controller is deallocated, so per-screen state that must survive has to live outside it (in a model object), not in the controller.
Pushing or presenting from a background thread crashes or silently drops the transition; all stack changes belong on the main actor.
Registering model callbacks as closures that capture the view controller strongly creates a retain cycle that keeps the screen and its whole view hierarchy alive after it is popped.
